Thou
thou
pron. (second person singular, nominative; rendering Hebrew 'attah, Greek su)
From Saxon þu, cognate with Latin tu, Greek su, Hebrew 'attah. The Authorized Version keeps the old English singular where modern versions have flattened everything into you. Thou is not elevated speech; it is exact speech — it means one person and not two.

Biblical Definition

Thou is the second person singular of the Authorized Version, and it carries information that modern English has thrown away. Hebrew and Greek both distinguish the one from the many, and the KJV translators preserved that distinction in English: thou, thee, thy, thine for one person; ye, you, your, yours for more than one. The doctrinal weight of this is not small. The Decalogue reads “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Exodus 20:3) — singular, so that no Israelite could hide inside the congregation and treat the commandment as addressed to the nation in bulk. God calls the fallen man out from the trees by the singular: “Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9). Christ finds all three disciples sleeping in the garden and rebukes one by name: “Simon, sleepest thou?” And Peter's confession is singular on both sides — “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). Every commandment, every promise, and every summons in the singular lands on a particular person who must answer for himself. The pronoun is a doctrine of personal accountability built into the grammar.

Webster 1828 Definition

The second person singular pronoun, nominative case; used of one person only, as distinguished from ye and you, which are plural. In Scripture it marks the commandment, the promise, and the summons as addressed to a particular person rather than to a congregation in the mass.

expand to see more

THOU, pron. [Sax. þu; L. tu; Gr. su.] The second personal pronoun, in the singular number; the nominative case.

2. It is used only in addressing a single person, and is opposed to ye and you, which are plural.

3. In common English discourse it has become disused, and you is substituted for the singular as well as the plural; but thou is retained in the solemn style, and in address to God.

4. THOU, v.t. To treat with familiarity; to address as thou.

5. In Scripture, Thou shalt have no other gods before me, Exo. 20; Where art thou? Gen. 3; Thou art the Christ, Matt. 16.

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:3 — "Thou shalt have no other gods before me."

Genesis 3:9 — "And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?"

Matthew 16:16 — "And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God."

Mark 14:37 — "And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?"

Modern Corruption

The common notion that thou is stately, formal, God-only language has the truth exactly backwards: it is the plain, familiar, singular form. What is genuinely lost when it goes is not reverence but precision — the ability to tell whether Scripture is speaking to one soul or to a whole church.

expand to see more

The living misuse is a well-meaning one. Because thou survives in English chiefly in prayer and in the Authorized Version, readers infer that it must be an honorific — a special reverential register reserved for addressing God. Historically it is the opposite. Thou was the ordinary, intimate, singular address used between equals, to children, and to servants; you was the deferential plural borrowed for polite address to a superior. The KJV therefore has God addressed as Thou not because the pronoun is grand, but because there is one God and the worshipper speaks to Him directly. To read reverence into the form is to miss the intimacy that is actually there.

The graver loss is interpretive. When every thou and every ye is rendered you, the English reader can no longer see what the Hebrew and Greek plainly show. He cannot tell that the Lord's promise to Peter in Luke 22:32 shifts between the plural and the singular within two verses, nor that the great commands of the Decalogue are singular and inescapable. Modern translators did not remove the distinction out of malice; they removed it because English usage had already died. But what died was a real instrument of exegesis, and the reader who keeps the Authorized Version keeps the instrument.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'attah (masculine) and 'att (feminine), the singular you; Greek su, the second person singular, with its emphatic use when the verb already carries the person; Saxon þu, the English ancestor.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'attah (H859) — thou, masculine singular; the form of address in every singular commandment of the Decalogue.

Hebrew 'att (H859) — thou, feminine singular; used of Israel as the wife of the LORD and of individual women.

Greek su (G4771) — thou; when written out rather than carried by the verb ending it is emphatic, as in Matthew 16:16.

Greek humeis (G5210) — ye, the plural counterpart; the contrast between the two is invisible in modern English.

Saxon þu — the Old English singular, cognate with Latin tu; the direct ancestor of the KJV form.

Usage

"Of the singular commandment binding each man alone: Thou shalt have no other gods before me (Exodus 20:3)."

"Of God summoning the individual sinner: Where art thou? (Genesis 3:9)."

"Of personal confession before Christ: Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16)."
